To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) there are difficulties to provide end-of-life care in the ICU; (ii) the difficulties can be grouped into three categories, which are: academic and cultural difficulties, structural architectural difficulties, and psychoemotional difficulties; and (iii) there is a lack of training in end-of-life care for nurses.

the nursing team needs training in palliative care through guidelines or protocols and the development of coping strategies together with an organizational change in the ICU aimed at the terminal care of critically ill patients and attention to the family.

nurses working in ICUs need training on end-of-life care using guidelines or protocols and developing strategies to cope with it, together with a change in the organization of the ICU oriented to terminal care of critically ill patients and to family care.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the difficulties experienced by the nursing staff in providing end-of-life care to critically ill patients.
the difficulties that nursing staff face in the ICU when they have to provide end-of-life care for critically ill patients.
the identification of the difficulties perceived by the nursing staff in caring for patients in the terminal stages of life, within the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

nurses in the intensive care unit are in a position of conflict, because they are trained to save lives, but when this possibility is lost, they are not prepared to face the end of life, which causes emotional distancing and difficulties in providing care.

nursing professionals need training on end-of-life care using guidelines or protocols and developing strategies for dealing with this situation, together with a change in the organization of the ICU oriented towards the terminal care of seriously ill patients and attention to their families.

the nursing staff needs to be trained in end-of-life care by using protocols and guides and by developing coping strategies, as well as a change in the organization of the ICU oriented to terminal care of the critical patients and to family care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nursing staff in the ICU needs to be trained in end-of-life care through the use of guides or protocols, and the development of strategies to face the end-of-life care.
the nurses have a need for more training in palliative care, and they need to be more involved in the process of decision-making in the ICU.

we have found that the main difficulties that nursing staff face when providing end-of-life care are related to the curative orientation and the lack of training in end-of-life care, as well as the lack of space and intimacy for patients and their families during the last moments of their lives.
The main takeaway from our work is that

nurses need to receive training in the care of dying patients, and that the intensive care unit (ICU) should be reorganized so that the care of dying is not seen as a burden, but rather as part of its daily activity.
we need a change in the organization of the ICU, with a focus on the care of terminal patients and their families.
we should not only consider the patient’s perspective but also the perspective of the healthcare providers, especially nurses, in order to improve the end-of-life care.
